channel.title: Comments on: Is Rock Conscious?
channel.description: taoism, taoist thought, buddha, yoga, tai chi, shakuhachi

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
In reply to <a href="/2011/08/10/is-rock-conscious/comment-page-1/#comment-1704224">Bob Willard</a>.
Gurdjieff's view that "the vast majority of humans are not fully conscious" reveals the limited scope of his understanding of nature as a whole, and to an elitist viewpoint that originates in a deep personal insecurity.
Words and the beliefs we build out of them gain their meaning in our emotions. As living being seeking to survive, we are innately insecure. We fear loss, failure, death, discomfort, hunger, isolation... you name it. These deep seated emotions--desires and worries, and everything in between--drive our thoughts and judgments.
So, what does this have to do with Gurdjieff and consciousness? Words are essentially human cognitive constructs that allows us to differentiate experience. Each individual uses their experience to give meaning to the words they use to think and communicate. The meaning someone gives to words offers a glimpse into their core nature--their emotions. Words and the thoughts they convey simply reflect the mind of the thinker. You could say, "Word meaning lies in the mind of the beholder". In this case, Gurdjieff shows that he regards himself as superior..., which is driven by deep inner insecurity.
Words are a completely arbitrary construct, yet core insecurity compels us to take the meanings we give them seriously enough to make us feel we 'know' reality. Thus, we lock ourselves into an arbitrary self- virtuous virtual reality that offers us some fleeting emotional stability in the changeable shifting sands of reality.
Interestingly, the more fleeting the stability feels, the more one needs to espouse the story. The belief becomes its own proof, if you will. You can see this throughout human culture: from politics and religion to science and everything in between. We humans excel at self-deception. :)

Yes, well put. Our sense of time is hugely distorted, but naturally and biologically so. For us, this becomes problematic due to our cognitive ability to imagine a past, a present and a future. This cognitive ability distorts every perception, as chapter 71 so wisely puts it.... "Realizing I don’t’ know is better; not knowing this knowing is disease"

item.title: By: MosesK
item.dc:creator: MosesK
item.description: I've always thought about this topic, mine, however was kind of broadened to take mountains to be living beings. They do age, after all. It's just that the process happens so slowly and so ordinarily, that nothing seems out of place. I actually thought about it this way; the faster we live, the faster we die. Compared to a mountain or a rock, we live our lives very fast. However, compared to a housefly, then our lives are lived agonizingly slowly. Akin to houseflies, compared to mountains, then our lives fade very fast.

item.title: By: carl
item.dc:creator: carl
item.description:
Yes, first we pin ourselves down with word meanings (the core preconceptions), then box ourselves in with them. My worse cognitive error was in judging our species by our own ‘high’ ideals. I couldn’t help conclude that our species was like a cancer on the planet.
The correlation process went a long way towards freeing me from word meaning. Not entirely of course, otherwise I wouldn’t be able to think or write anything. The process just helped me take it all with a grain of salt… kind of like seeing the whole forest rather than being trapped by the trees.
Re your professor’s example: How we define “sensation” narrows what we are capable of seeing as possessing sensation. If we define sensation as something that requires nerve cells, for example, then neither rocks nor fire qualify. If we define consciousness as requiring sensation, then neither qualifies as being conscious either. Definition have a way of becoming a our self fulfilling prophecy.
I suppose we do all this to limit the infinite mystery down to manageable bite sized digestible chunks. That’s fine, Now, if we could only learn this is what we were doing, rather than thinking we truly know, we wouldn’t shot ourselves in the foot as much.
Oh well, :-)

item.title: By: Dan Littler
item.dc:creator: Dan Littler
item.description: This reminds me of something my philosophy lecturer at uni used to say; that fire is alive, according to the conditions of living organisms taught in schools. Fire moves, respires, grows, reproduces, takes nourishment and excretes. Some of these are a little sketchy, of course, but you can see how it could easily be argued. The only one missing is sensation, and I can be no more certain that fire doesn't feel as I can that, well, rocks don't. That is to say, we can only make an educated guess (based on preconceptions).
